prompt: A system adds one more independent on/off feature flag. Every old configuration remains allowed with the new flag either off or on. What happens to the number of configurations?

options.explanation: There is a new choice for every old configuration, not just one extra configuration.

options.text: It stays the same because the flag has only two values.
options.explanation: Two choices create distinct versions of every old configuration.
Each old configuration has exactly two extensions.

options.text: It doubles only if the all-off configuration is excluded.
options.explanation: The power set includes the empty subset; excluding it changes the counting problem.

workedExample: Pair each old configuration with two new ones: new flag off, and new flag on. Different old configurations cannot produce the same extended configuration, and every new configuration comes from one old configuration. This establishes doubling without calculating a large power.

prompt: A loop visits every five-bit mask and keeps a mask only when `bin(mask).count("1") == 2`. What does the filter select?

options.text: All subsets of the five items.
options.explanation: Masks with other numbers of set bits fail the filter.
A bitmask records membership, not selection order.

options.text: Pairs that can select the same item twice.
options.explanation: One bit cannot represent two copies of its item.

options.text: Exactly the subsets containing two distinct items.
options.explanation: Each set bit selects one position, and the filter requires exactly two.

workedExample: Assign one item to each bit position. A 1 means included and a 0 means excluded. Counting the 1s counts selected items. Swapping the order in which two items were selected would leave the same mask, so this models an unordered pair.
